title: Remove the Cells, or the Pigment?

scenes.tts: A mouse has no working rods or cones. Even so, it can tell a striped screen from a grey one. That is the finding in mice lacking rod and cone signalling. So which cells are doing the seeing? One candidate is a small set of retinal ganglion cells. They carry their own light pigment, called melanopsin.
scenes.visual: Mouse retina chain: rod and cone, bipolar, ganglion cell, brain. Rod and cone crossed out. Striped and grey screens. Question mark, then the ganglion cell lights up with melanopsin.
scenes.narration: A mouse has no working rods or cones. Even so, it can tell a striped screen from a grey one. That is the finding in mice lacking rod and cone signalling. So which cells are doing the seeing? One candidate is a small set of retinal ganglion cells. They carry their own light pigment, called melanopsin.

scenes.tts: These cells are called intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells, or ip R G Cs. An ip R G C makes its own light response with melanopsin. It also relays signals that rods and cones send through bipolar cells. So it has two jobs. Hold on to that. The rest of the film depends on it.

scenes.visual: One large ipRGC. Green route: own melanopsin response. Blue route: rod and cone signals via a bipolar cell.
scenes.narration: These cells are called intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells, or ipRGCs. An ipRGC makes its own light response with melanopsin. It also relays signals that rods and cones send through bipolar cells. So it has two jobs. Hold on to that. The rest of the film depends on it.

scenes.tts: Now the first result. Mice lacking rod and cone signalling were able to discriminate a grating from an equally bright grey. Cells labelled with a melanopsin reporter heavily innervated a brain target, the d L G N. So these cells give a route for coarse pattern information. It is not normal acuity. Those mice managed zero point one six cycles per degree. Wild type mice managed zero point five five.

Those mice managed 0.16 cycles per degree. Wild type mice managed 0.55.

scenes.tts: The second result comes from a different experiment. Mice lacking melanopsin showed deficits in contrast sensitivity. Both results come from mice. That sounds like the answer. But look at what was removed. Taking out the pigment removes one job. Taking out the cells removes both.
scenes.visual: Panel one: ipRGC with melanopsin crossed out, relay route intact. Panel two: ipRGC removed, both routes crossed.
scenes.narration: The second result comes from a different experiment. Mice lacking melanopsin showed deficits in contrast sensitivity. Both results come from mice. That sounds like the answer. But look at what was removed. Taking out the pigment removes one job. Taking out the cells removes both.

scenes.tts: Now picture an ablation. Remove the cells, and the animal does worse. You have lost the melanopsin response and the rod and cone relay together. The experiment cannot say which one mattered. Ablation implicates the cells. It does not name the input. A task can fail without the pigment mattering.
scenes.visual: Cell removed, task impaired; both routes lost together; question marks over which route mattered.
scenes.narration: Now picture an ablation. Remove the cells, and the animal does worse. You have lost the melanopsin response and the rod and cone relay together. The experiment cannot say which one mattered. Ablation implicates the cells. It does not name the input. A task can fail without the pigment mattering.

scenes.tts: So how do you decide? Compare melanopsin knockouts with animals whose ip R G Cs are removed. Prefer an adult, timed manipulation, because loss during development can rewire targets. And remember the limits. These results come from mice, and grating discrimination is not normal acuity. Removing the cells and removing the pigment answer different questions.
